title: India Rejects Hague Court Ruling on Indus Waters Treaty as 'Illegal'
excerpt: India has dismissed the Permanent Court of Arbitration's latest award on the Kishenganga and Ratle hydroelectric projects, calling the tribunal illegally constituted and its rulings void.
body:
• India has rejected the Hague-based Court of Arbitration's latest award on the Kishenganga and Ratle hydroelectric projects, calling the tribunal "illegal" and its decisions "per se void."
  • The Court ruled that India's decision to place the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance does not strip the tribunal of jurisdiction over the dispute.
  • India placed the treaty in abeyance after the Pahalgam terror attack in April 2025, linking its reinstatement to Pakistan ending support for cross-border terrorism.
  • The August 8 award addressed design requirements for run-of-river hydroelectric plants on the Western Rivers — India boycotted the proceedings entirely.

India has firmly rejected the latest ruling by a Hague-based Court of Arbitration on its Kishenganga and Ratle hydroelectric projects in Jammu and Kashmir, calling the tribunal illegally constituted and its awards devoid of legal standing.

Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India's position remains unchanged. "India has never accepted the legality, legitimacy, or competence of the so-called Court of Arbitration. Its pronouncements are therefore without jurisdiction, devoid of legal standing, and have no bearing on India's rights of utilisation of waters," Jaiswal said at a weekly media briefing, according to ANI.

"India has never recognised the existence in law of this so-called Court of Arbitration, and India's position has all along been that the constitution of this so-called arbitral body is in itself a serious breach of the Indus Waters Treaty."

— India's Ministry of External Affairs

The Dispute

The standoff centers on Pakistan's objections to certain design elements of two run-of-river hydroelectric projects — Kishenganga and Ratle — that India is constructing on tributaries of the Western Rivers allocated to Pakistan under the Indus Waters Treaty. Pakistan initiated arbitration proceedings through the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, while India simultaneously sought resolution through a Neutral Expert appointed by the World Bank.

India has boycotted the proceedings from the outset, arguing that the treaty prohibits parallel dispute resolution mechanisms and that the Court's constitution was itself a breach of the 1960 agreement. Despite India's absence, the PCA proceeded, ruling in July 2023 that it had jurisdiction to hear the case.

Two Key Rulings

The tribunal has delivered two significant awards this year. On June 27, it issued a supplemental award ruling that India's decision to place the treaty in abeyance "does not limit" the Court's competence. The Court found that the treaty does not permit unilateral abeyance or suspension, stating that it "provides for its continuation in force until terminated by mutual consent."

On August 8, the five-member panel — chaired by Professor Sean D. Murphy of the United States — issued an "Award on Issues of General Interpretation" addressing design requirements for run-of-river hydroelectric plants on the Western Rivers. The ruling was unanimous except for one section on maximum pondage, decided 4-1. While the award did not apply its findings directly to the Kishenganga or Ratle projects, the Court said it remains seized of those matters.

India's Position

India placed the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance after the Pahalgam terror attack on April 22, 2025, which killed 26 tourists. New Delhi has linked the treaty's reinstatement to Pakistan "credibly and irrevocably" ending its support for cross-border terrorism.

The MEA described the arbitration as a "charade at Pakistan's behest" and "yet another desperate attempt by it to escape accountability for its role as the global epicenter of terrorism." India has argued that as a sovereign nation, its decision to suspend the treaty is an exercise of its rights under international law and that no tribunal has jurisdiction to examine it.

Pakistan Welcomes Ruling

Pakistan has welcomed the Court's decisions. Its Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the supplemental award a vindication of Islamabad's position that the treaty remains valid and operational. "We urge India to immediately resume the normal functioning of the Indus Waters Treaty, and fulfil its treaty obligations, wholly and faithfully," Pakistan said.

What Comes Next

The Court will determine the next steps after consulting both parties, though India's continued refusal to participate makes enforcement a significant challenge. The dispute underscores the deep freeze in India-Pakistan relations following the Pahalgam attack and raises questions about the future of one of the world's oldest water-sharing agreements — a treaty that has survived three wars and decades of hostility between the two nuclear-armed neighbors.
